```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
library(idiographic)
data(srl)
```

Repeated-measures data are usually transformed before modelling. This
vignette covers three transformations: separating each variable into its
between-person and within-person parts, creating lagged variables, and
removing time trends. Each transformation is computed separately for each
person and in time order. The examples use the 36 learners in the `srl`
data, each observed on 156 days.

## Within-person and between-person decomposition

Each repeated measure has two parts. The between-person part is the stable
average across all occasions. The within-person part is the fluctuation of
each occasion around that stable average. Differences between persons in
their stable averages form the between-person variation; the fluctuations
form the within-person variation. An analysis of the raw scores, whether
across all occasions or at a single occasion, mixes the two, and its result
can resemble the within-person association, the between-person association,
or neither, depending on how much of each variable is stable and how much
fluctuates. Separating the two parts allows each association to be estimated
on its own.

For a variable $x$ observed for person $i$ at occasion $t$, `split_levels()`
computes the between-person part as the mean of that person's observed
values,
$$\bar{x}_i = \frac{1}{T_i}\sum_{t=1}^{T_i} x_{it},$$
where $T_i$ is the number of occasions on which $x$ was observed. The
within-person part is the deviation of each observation from that mean,
$x_{it} - \bar{x}_i$. The two parts sum to the original score. For efficacy,
the between-person part is stored as `efficacy_between` and the
within-person part as `efficacy_within`.

```{r decompose}
split_levels(srl, id = "name", vars = "efficacy", time = "day", keep_all = FALSE) |> head()
```

To see how effort relates to each part, both parts are used as predictors in
the same regression. The slope of `efficacy_within` shows how effort changes
on days when a learner's efficacy is above or below that learner's average.
The slope of `efficacy_between` shows how effort differs between learners
with higher and lower average efficacy. `fit_within_between()` performs the
split and the regression in one step. Because each learner contributes many
days, its standard errors are adjusted for the repeated observations of the
same learner.

```{r within-between}
wb_fit <- fit_within_between(srl, y = "effort", x = "efficacy", id = "name", time = "day")
coefs(wb_fit)
```

The within-person slope was 0.42 (95% CI 0.30 to 0.53). On days when a
learner's efficacy was 10 points above that learner's average, effort was
about 4 points higher. The between-person slope was 0.63 (95% CI 0.41 to
0.84). Learners whose average efficacy was 10 points higher reported about 6
points more effort on average. The between-person interval is wider because
it rests on 36 learners, while the within-person slope draws on all of their
days.

Whether the two slopes differ is tested directly by their difference, which
`contextual()` reports.

```{r contextual}
contextual(wb_fit)
```

The between-person slope exceeded the within-person slope by 0.21 (95% CI
0.003 to 0.42, p = .047). The interval barely excludes zero, so the evidence
that the two slopes differ is weak.

## Lagged variables

A lagged variable holds the value of a variable on the preceding occasion.
With `lag = 1`, the column `efficacy_lag1` contains, in each row, the
learner's efficacy on the previous day. Lagged variables allow a model to
test whether a state on one day predicts an outcome on the next, for example
whether efficacy yesterday predicts effort today.

Lags are computed within persons, so the first occasion of each person has a
missing lagged value, as shown below for the first days of Aisha.

```{r lags}
preprocess_panel(srl, id = "name", time = "day", vars = "efficacy", lag = 1, keep_all = FALSE) |> head()
```

A lag refers to the preceding occasion regardless of the time elapsed
between occasions. For irregularly spaced occasions, `lag_max_gap` sets the
lagged value to missing when the preceding occasion lies further back than a
specified interval.

## Detrending

`preprocess_panel(detrend = "person")` removes the linear time trend of each
person's series when the trend is significant at `detrend_alpha` (0.05 by
default). The presence of trends is assessed beforehand with the trend
estimates reported by `describe_persons()`.

```{r trends}
trends <- describe_persons(srl, id = "name", time = "day", vars = "efficacy:organizing", detail = "full")
summary(trends)
```

Across the nine variables, 16 of the 324 person-by-variable series (4.9%)
had a significant linear trend, the proportion expected from false positives at the 0.05 level if no
series trended. Detrending these data would therefore modify a small number
of series largely at random. Detrending is warranted when significant trends
are considerably more frequent than the significance level, or when the
design implies a trend, as in intervention or developmental studies. Series
without a fixed slope, such as random walks, require differencing, which
`preprocess(detrend = "auto")` applies to the affected series only.

## Centring and scaling

Person-centring (`center = "person"`) retains only the within-person part
and discards the between-person part; `split_levels()` retains both, so the
two options are not combined. Person scaling (`scale = "person"`) divides
each person's values by that person's standard deviation, which places
persons who fluctuate to different degrees on a common scale. Grand scaling
(`scale = "grand"`) uses a single standard deviation for all persons.

`preprocess_panel()` and `split_levels()` compute these quantities from all
occasions of each person. Model functions that hold out later occasions for
testing, such as `fit_within_between()`, compute them from the training
occasions only.
